Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

spax 0.3.1

Patch release. Poisson flow fits are now maximum likelihood estimates; saved fits from 0.3.0 keep working.

  • Poisson fits in fit_allocation() now floor modelled counts at 1e-250 instead of 1e-9 (set by loss_args = list(eps = ...)). The old floor capped the loss of positive counts that the model puts almost no weight on, such as residents registered far from home, so a flow fit was not the Poisson maximum likelihood estimate and moved with the floor: in the Cornwall registration guide the Gaussian scale changes from 4.36 to 4.59 minutes and the outside weight from 0.0176 to 0.0273. Facility-total estimates are unaffected. fit_allocation() warns and check_allocation() reports cells with positive counts that are still modelled below the floor (for example counts on absent edges or at a facility with zero supply); check_allocation() also reports them for saved fits made with the old floor. compare_allocations() treats a saved Poisson fit without a stored floor as using 1e-9, and compares fits with different floors when neither floor changes either loss.

  • Version 0.3.0 is archived on Zenodo: cite it as doi:10.5281/zenodo.23438612. doi:10.5281/zenodo.23438611 refers to all versions. citation("spax") gives the reference.

spax 0.3.0

First release that includes the experimental allocation workflow. Experimental functions may change in later versions; record the package version when reproducing an analysis.

  • Fixed: with loss = "poisson" and gradient = TRUE, the analytic gradient is now the gradient of the floored loss. A modelled count below the floor (eps, 1e-9) adds a constant to the loss, and it now adds nothing to the gradient; before, it kept the slope 1 - y / eps, which misled the optimizer on flow targets with positive counts where the model puts almost no flow (starts that stopped apart, or line-search failures). Fits whose modelled counts all stay above the floor are unchanged; the Poisson loss itself is unchanged, so saved fits keep working.

  • New experimental decay_kernel() declares a distance decay kernel as plain data: a built-in kernel by name, or your own function of distance and sigma, kept as the exact text of its code (comments and layout are not kept) together with a name, a label for what sigma means, bounds on sigma and fixed extra arguments. The function is run on a grid of distances when it is declared, and one that returns weights that are not finite, nonnegative and non-increasing is refused. A declaration can replace the method string in calc_decay() and in the decay_params of the FCA functions (spax_e2sfca(), spax_m2sfca(), spax_3sfca() and spax_huff2sfca()); a built-in declaration behaves exactly like its string.

  • clm_allocation() accepts a declared kernel as family. Fitting, evaluation, requested-location prediction, check_allocation() and compare_allocations() work with it, and so does bootstrap_allocation() when the kernel is smooth in sigma. A kernel declared with smooth = FALSE (a cutoff or a step, for example) can be evaluated and used for prediction but not fitted. Results that use a declared kernel save its code in a new version of the prediction snapshot (spax_clm_prediction_v2), so using a saved fit runs that code and saved fits should be read only from sources you trust. Snapshots of the built-in kernels are unchanged. Printed and summarized fits now label sigma by its meaning for the kernel, for example gaussian (sigma = travel scale).

  • A declared kernel is held to more checks. The function must be elementwise (the weight of a distance may not depend on the other distances or on their order), because it receives a vector or a matrix of distances. sigma must be positive, as well as inside the declared bounds, in calc_decay(), fitting and evaluation, requested-location prediction and when a saved snapshot is read (“ decay requires positive sigma”). The check at declaration also runs the function at a positive lower bound and at a finite upper bound of sigma, and calc_decay() refuses a negative or non-finite weight at a finite distance, which the grid of the declaration cannot rule out. A SpatRaster is read into memory when a declared kernel is applied to it.

  • The finite-difference derivatives that fitting and bootstrap_allocation() use no longer step outside the bounds of a model’s parameters. Next to a bound, for example the lower bound of a declared kernel, they use a one-sided difference. The central step used to leave the bounds there: a fit then fell back from its analytic gradient without a message, and bootstrap_allocation() could stop with an error about theta being outside its bounds or lose draws that lie on a bound. Results for the built-in kernels do not change, except that a parameter closer to zero than one step (about 1e-6) no longer errors. If the score diagnostic of the original fit cannot be computed, bootstrap_allocation() now refuses intervals with the status original_score_failed instead of stopping.

  • Fitting keeps trial parameter values inside the bounds of the model’s parameters and the estimate inside the search bounds, also where exp(log(bound)) rounds just outside a bound (for example 7.6). A fit on its search bound is then refused by bootstrap_allocation() as a boundary estimate instead of failing with “invalid saved fit bounds”, and a declared kernel can be fitted on a declared bound. Other estimates do not change.

  • bootstrap_allocation() adds a coverage_note to its result, and prints it, for every model other than built-in Gaussian decay with fitted sigma and v0 and kappa and beta equal to 1, the case the coverage study covered: other kernels, a fitted beta and other values of kappa and beta use the same procedure without a separate coverage study. Results for the studied case are unchanged and have no note.

  • New experimental spax_3sfca() computes the three-step floating catchment area index. Each origin first divides its demand among the facilities with selection weights, a facility’s share of the origin’s decay weights, and both steps then use the product of the decay and selection weights. The selection weights can use a different decay from the one that weights distance (selection_params). Because both steps share one kernel, the index returns the total supply of the facilities that gather demand.

  • New experimental spax_huff2sfca() is the same calculation with Huff selection probabilities, which also depend on facility attractiveness (by default the single supply measure; alpha is its exponent). With alpha = 0 it equals spax_3sfca(). Several supply measures need an explicit attractiveness.

  • New experimental calc_demand() computes demand from population groups (for example age bands) and group-specific rates, times a common scale. With a total-population grid, each cell’s group composition is applied to its total, which reconciles gridded group and total products that do not sum exactly.

  • New experimental calc_travel_time() computes continuous least-cost travel times from facilities to every cell of an analysis grid over a friction surface (such as the Malaria Atlas Project motorized friction surface), with optional barriers, a maximum time and bilinear or averaging transfer of the friction surface to the grid. The result is the origin-by-facility matrix prepare_allocation() accepts, with the matching cell index, or one raster layer per facility.

  • New experimental compare_allocations() summarizes several fitted allocations side by side (contact, capacity per contact, spread of contact, agreement with observed counts and loss) and, with zones, lists the zones whose reporting class changes. Loss differences are reported only when the observed targets, loss, demand, supply and travel times are identical; travel times are verified when the models are supplied. Saved coverage also gains as.data.frame(type = "zones", zones = ...), which aggregates cells to zones with demand and contacting-demand weights.

  • New experimental check_allocation() compares a fitted allocation with an allocation without distance decay (within the prepared travel support) and one that shares counts by capacity alone, on the same loss, and reports the one-way trip lengths each implies. When capacity closely tracks the observed facility counts, the counts alone may not identify distance decay; the check says so instead of leaving it to be discovered. A fitted attractiveness exponent is re-optimized in both comparators. It reports only and never changes the fit.

  • The no-decay comparator of check_allocation() is exact: it is the same model with a constant kernel (weight 1 on every finite travel time), whatever kernel the model uses, instead of a built-in kernel at an extreme parameter value. Its reported parameters no longer include sigma, which that allocation does not use: parameters$no_decay holds the re-optimized parameters other than sigma, and the table reads no decay, followed by the re-optimized v0 (and beta) when the model fits them. Reported losses move by at most about 1e-8 relative for travel times in minutes.

  • summary.spax() coverage now counts only cells with a value, so cells outside the study area (such as sea) no longer lower it, and reports the share of those cells with accessibility above zero. It previously divided the number of cells with a value by every cell in the raster.

  • Printed corrected CLM fits now show model: clm instead of the internal family name huff.

  • A fit saved with saveRDS() and read back is no longer rejected by bootstrap_allocation() or reported as not like for like by compare_allocations() when the package keeps source references (in a development load, or with R_KEEP_PKG_SOURCE=yes). The saved copy of the package’s Poisson loss function then differed from the original only in those references, which the comparison now ignores.

  • The calc_decay(), sample_pmf() and rasterize_demand() examples now run; the last uses the Cornwall small areas.

  • The README and the guides now use the bundled Cornwall GP data, with real maps, instead of generated grids. Only the facility bootstrap guide keeps a generated network, where the true parameters are known.

  • The guides now follow one reader journey. vignette("spax") is a short Get started guide; a new vignette("cornwall-data") introduces the example data once, before data-prep; the FCA guides are fca-methods, e2sfca-steps and grid-resolution (formerly spax-101 to spax-104); and the allocation track runs from model-choice through allocation-workflow to a separate facility-bootstrap guide. The pkgdown site groups the articles under these headings and sets printed output apart from code.

  • Breaking: the Thailand Health Region 12 example data have been removed from the package, because their redistribution terms could not be fully confirmed. All examples and tests now use the open Cornwall GP data.

    Removed Use instead
    hos_iscr.tif, phc_iscr.tif (travel time to facilities) read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")
    u5pd.tif (population grid) read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
    hc12_hos, hc12_phc (facilities and supply) cornwall_gp
    bound0, bound1 (boundaries) cornwall_lsoa
    hos_iscvec (isochrone polygons) no direct replacement

    The package is about 1 MB instead of about 27 MB. Analyses that need the old objects should load them from a saved copy of an earlier spax version.

  • transform_pmf(), transform_likelihood() and transform_demand() now accept SpatVector input. Their column check read a one-column data frame, so every column was rejected; the extent check also rejected single and collinear points. transform_demand(full_output = TRUE) no longer requires an undocumented id column, and transform_demand() now warns when an area covers no grid cell, because its count would be dropped.

  • Fixes in the FCA and PMF tools:

    • rasterize_demand() without a prior now uses the documented uniform prior over the non-missing cells of the template’s first layer. It previously used the observations’ own PMF, so the posterior was proportional to the squared counts. standardize = TRUE is now refused, because z-scores are not a likelihood, as is an all-missing template.
    • update_pmf(normalize = FALSE, density = TRUE) no longer scales the posterior twice.
    • Point input to transform_pmf(), transform_likelihood() and rasterize_demand() now adds up points that fall in the same cell, ignoring missing values; only the last point’s value was kept, so counts were lost. Polygon values are still copied to every cell they cover.
    • transform_pmf(), update_pmf() and rasterize_demand() accept multi-layer rasters and normalize each layer separately; they previously failed with “the condition has length > 1”. update_pmf() requires matching layer counts unless one side has a single layer.
    • sample_pmf() takes size from the rounded total of raw density input, as documented, when only prob is given; a PMF input still needs size. Multi-layer input is refused with a clear message.
    • calc_normalize() refuses a missing numeric ref_value (NA_real_, NaN) with a clear error instead of a base R error.
    • calc_normalize() on a SpatRaster accepts a numeric ref_value for the "reference" method; it previously failed inside terra::ifel(). The documentation now states that rasters are normalized cell by cell across layers.
    • calc_decay() accepts integer distances such as 1:5; logical matrices and classed numerics such as units objects are refused.
    • summary.spax() keeps every requested quantile (it kept only the first), and custom quantiles print with percentage labels.
    • sample_pmf() rejects an n that is not a single non-negative whole number (also in snap mode) instead of returning an empty raster or drawing a truncated count, and an all-NA input gets the PMF error instead of a base R error.
    • spax_2sfca() validates threshold with a message that names it; NA and NULL, which gave all-NaN results or the binary default, are refused.
    • print() of an FCA result whose decay_params$method is a function no longer fails in cat(); it prints custom function, and a declared kernel prints its name.
    • print() of an FCA result whose decay_params$sigma is a raster (a variable catchment) no longer fails in sprintf(); it prints variable (raster).

  • calc_normalize() and calc_choice() now refuse negative weights (outside snap mode); they previously divided by the remaining sum and returned negative “probabilities”. A custom calc_normalize() method still receives its input unchecked.

  • clm_allocation() requires fit_v0 and fit_beta to be TRUE or FALSE; other values such as "yes" were silently treated as FALSE.

  • ?calc_decay documents each kernel’s formula and the sigma used when none is given, and notes that power decay is infinite at distance 0.

  • fit_allocation() and bootstrap_allocation() no longer force a full garbage collection before every fit: the internal fit timer used system.time(), which collects garbage first by default. Results are unchanged; repeated fits run faster (the package tests take half as long).

  • The update_pmf(), transform_demand() and calc_normalize() examples now run; the first two previously referred to an undefined object.

  • The allocation-workflow vignette now loads its full 399-attempt bootstrap result from vignettes/allocation-bootstrap.rds instead of recomputing it, cutting the vignette rebuild from about 200 s to under 30 s. The printed call, seed and every reported number are unchanged; the vignette stops if the stored result does not match the live fit. Regenerate it with data-raw/precompute-vignette-bootstrap.R whenever bootstrap or fitting code changes. A test now runs the real bootstrap engine for three attempts.

  • New open example data for the 55 GP practices of NHS Cornwall and Isles of Scilly: cornwall_gp, cornwall_lsoa, cornwall_flows, cornwall_travel, and the cornwall_pop.tif and cornwall_gp_travel.tif grids read with read_spax_example(). All sources are openly licensed (Open Government Licence v3.0, Creative Commons Attribution); see inst/COPYRIGHTS. The data are rebuilt reproducibly by data-raw/cornwall_gp.R from pinned sources.

  • The supported minimum is R 4.4.0, with testthat 3.2.0 for tests. This is the dependency and testing policy for the development branch. CI targets release R on Linux, Windows and macOS, plus Linux R-devel and the exact minimum R version. Existing public FCA calling semantics are unchanged by this compatibility floor.

  • Tutorials now use portable generated examples; live routing is optional and is not executed during routine builds. A model-choice guide connects the public FCA and experimental allocation workflows. The full allocation example retains all 399 bootstrap attempts and its existing statistical reporting rules.

  • Removed the unused bench and fasterize packages from Suggests after the portable tutorial conversion.

  • Public FCA functions remain supported, including independent accessibility indicators from multiple supply columns. Their equations and normalization choices are unchanged by the experimental allocation interface.

  • Six experimental functions provide a corrected static CLM workflow: prepare_allocation(), clm_allocation(), fit_allocation(), evaluate_allocation(), predict_allocation() and bootstrap_allocation(). Preparation checks IDs, units declarations and support. Fitting retains explicit starts and diagnostics; prediction uses saved facility loads.

  • Allocation probabilities, modeled counts and supply attribution have distinct meanings. Requested predictions distinguish unknown travel from absent connections and expose validity and support flags.

  • The conditional facility-case bootstrap supports a static CLM with a fitted outside mass, fitted to complete whole facility counts. The decay kernel can be built in or declared, if it is smooth in sigma, and beta can be fixed or fitted. Its intervals require the declared observation assumptions and a complete 399-attempt run; refusals, failed attempts and incomplete results remain available for inspection. Coverage was evaluated for Gaussian decay with fitted sigma and v0; other kernels and a fitted beta use the same procedure without a separate coverage study.

  • Saved-result methods provide parameter, bootstrap, regional and cell tables, summaries and plots without rerunning fitting or resampling. The allocation article demonstrates a supply scenario, export and reload.

  • Package help now explains compatibility with public FCA and older private allocation results. Older objects may require regeneration for current prediction or reporting; huff_decay results must not be relabeled as corrected CLM outputs.
